# **Changelog** {#changelog}

## **Updates since Phase 1** {#updates-since-phase-1}

### **Formatting of Phase 1 Document** {#formatting-of-phase-1-document}

* Change: Converted list-style answers into paragraph-style responses.  
* Reason: Addressed the professor’s feedback that Phase 1 should use narrative paragraphs instead of lists. 

### **Vote Classification** {#vote-classification}

* Change: Reclassified Vote as a weak (associative) entity instead of a strong entity. Defined composite PK (user\_id, matchup\_id, entry\_id) with cast\_at as a non-key attribute.   
* Reason: Vote cannot exist independently; it depends on User, MatchUp, and Entry, so it must be modeled as associative. 

### **Title Page** {#title-page}

* Change: Added all group members' full names and removed “Phase 1” specification from the title.   
* Reason: To follow project formatting requirements for final submission. 

### **User Primary Key Change** {#user-primary-key-change}

* Change: Changed the User relation so that ‘user\_id’ is the only primary key. ‘email’ is now a normal attribute instead of being part of the key.

* Reason: Ensures a stable system-generated identifier. This avoids problems if users change their email addresses and maintains proper database design.

## **Updates since Phase 2** {#updates-since-phase-2}

### **Removal of Matchup\_Entry Associative Entity** {#removal-of-matchup_entry-associative-entity}

* Change: Removed the Matchup\_Entry table and added entryA\_id and entryB\_id as foreign keys in the Matchup table.  
* Reason: Based on instructor feedback, this change simplifies the schema by representing both competing entries directly within Matchup, eliminating the need for an extra associative relation.

### **User Table Renamed** {#user-table-renamed}

* Change: Renamed the table from ‘User’ to 'Users’.  
* Reason: Avoided conflict with SQL reserved keywords and improved clarity in queries.

### **Constraint Adjustments** {#constraint-adjustments}

* Change: Added ‘Check’ constraints to prevent empty string values for key text attributes (displayname, email, password, and title).  
* Reason: Ensures data integrity and enforces required field validation at the database level.

### **Added ENUM Constraints** {#added-enum-constraints}

* Change: Introduced ENUM types for role, tourneystatus, and status columns.  
* Reason: Restricts possible values to a defined list (‘admin’, ‘player’, ‘guest’) for cleaner data and easier validation. 

### **Foreign Key and Relationship Validation** {#foreign-key-and-relationship-validation}

* Change: Explicitly defined all foreign keys between tables (users, tournament, entry, matchup, vote) in the tables.sql file.   
* Reason: Enforces referential integrity and ensures each record properly references its parent entity.

## **Updates since Phase 4** {#updates-since-phase-4}

### **User Table Enhancement** {#user-table-enhancement}

* Change: Added profile\_picture (VARCHAR) and bio (TEXT) columns to the users table.  
* Reason: To support enhanced social features in the GUI application. This addition allows the "Tournament Bracket" page to visually identify the host who created that specific tournament with a profile picture and interactively display their bio via a tooltip on hover. It also enables users to customize their personal identity on the Profile Dashboard.

# **Phase 1 – Conceptual Database Design**

# **1.1 – Fact-Finding Techniques and Information Gathering**

## **1.1.1 – Introduction to the Enterprise/Organization**

We are designing a lightweight web platform that lets people create single-elimination tournaments (for sports teams, e-sports, movies, memes, etc.) and crowd‑vote the winners of each matchup. The platform serves organizers who set up tournaments and voters who cast votes during open rounds. Core activities include creating tournaments, adding entries, opening/closing rounds, voting on matchups, and advancing winners until a champion is selected.

## **1.1.2 – Motivation and Preliminary Research**

We chose a voting-bracket tournament because it’s fun, easy to demo, and feels like a simpler version of fantasy sports. Our intended audience is anyone who wants to vote on head-to-head matchups across different media (sports, movies, books, memes, etc.). We’re keeping a classic bracket format and plan to show an image and short description for each entry in the UI. Scope is intentionally aligned with what we covered in class (accounts/roles, 1:M and M:N via associative entities, and basic aggregation for vote counts).

For preliminary research, we looked at common bracket patterns and UI examples online, discussed voting windows and preventing duplicate votes, and thought through simple tie-breaker options. We also considered features like betting, but did not go through with it since that’s out of scope for this phase. Based on this, we’re sticking to single-elimination with exactly two entries per matchup and one vote per user per matchup, and for ties, we have decided to go with allowing the lower seed to advance for simplicity. 

## **1.1.3 – The Miniverse of Interest**

Our business aims to include user accounts, tournaments, entries, matchups per round, voting windows, votes, and winner advancement in the database. The business will intentionally exclude features such as live sports or movie APIs, player statistics, reseeding, double-elimination formats, betting, scoring systems, and user comments.

**Assumptions:**

The platform will support only single-elimination tournaments. In this format, each matchup eliminates one entry, with winners advancing in a straight bracket progression until a single champion remains. To maintain bracket symmetry, each tournament must have an even number of entries. Ties will be resolved in favor of the lower-seeded entry, removing ambiguity in determining winners. The platform will not support reseeding; winners will continue to advance according to the original bracket order, preserving the initial seeding logic and avoiding mid-tournament restructuring. Tournaments will be publicly available for browsing and participation, with basic role-based access control distinguishing between organizers and voting users.

**Sample Data plan:** 

The sample data plan will include approximately 6 to 10 users to exercise user account management and voting scenarios. Between 2 and 3 active tournaments will be created to test tournament operations and related features. Each tournament will include around 8 to 16 entries, representing teams, movies, or other contest subjects. During voting rounds, the system will process approximately 8 to 30 votes per round, simulating typical user engagement levels while supporting aggregation and validation testing.

**Risks/Out of Scope:** 

The platform will not integrate with external sports or live data APIs. Financial or payment processing systems will not be implemented, and no social or communication features, such as comments, chat, or forums, are planned. These topics are intentionally kept out of scope because they would create challenges with data consistency and add unnecessary complexity to the product’s design.

**Chosen Approach:**

We narrowed it down to single‑elimination brackets with an even number of entries for a predictable schema and simple advancement logic, considering the amount of time we have to work on the project throughout this class.

## **1.1.4 – User Groups, Data Access, and Operations**

**User Roles & Permissions:**

Organizers are registered users with the organizer role. They have access to their tournaments, entries, matchups, and vote tallies. They can create or edit tournaments, add entries, open and close rounds, generate next-round matchups, view results, and announce winners. Voters are registered users with the default role, while guests may only browse. Voters can access public tournaments, open matchups, and results. Their operations include casting exactly one vote per open matchup and viewing results once rounds have closed.

## **1.1.5 – Summary of Entities and Relationships**

* An Organizer can organize many Tournaments; each Tournament is organized by exactly one Organizer.  
* A Tournament can have many Entries; each Entry belongs to exactly one Tournament.  
* A Tournament can include many Matchups; each Matchup belongs to exactly one Tournament.  
* A Matchup pairs exactly two Entries (slots A and B) via the associative entity MatchUp\_Entry; an Entry can appear in many Matchups.  
* A User can cast at most one Vote per Matchup; a Matchup can receive many Votes; each Vote is for exactly one Entry that participates in that Matchup.

Business rules:

* Each Matchup has exactly two distinct slots {A, B}.  
* Vote(user, matchup) is unique; votes only count during the matchup’s open window.  
* A Vote.entry must be one of the two entries paired in that Matchup.

* Single‑elimination only; an even number of entries.

* Tie-breaker: If votes are tied at close, the lower seed advances.

* No reseeding; winners advance in bracket order.  
* Public tournaments; basic role‑based access.

# **1.2 – Conceptual Database Design**

## **1.2.1 – Entity Descriptions**

### **USER (strong)**

Attributes:

* user\_id — Unique identifier; unique: yes; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* email — Login email; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* password — Hashed password; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* display\_name — Public name; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* role — Authorization role {user, organizer, admin}; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.

### **TOURNAMENT (strong)**

Attributes:

* tournament\_id — Unique identifier; unique: yes; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* title — Tournament title; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* description — Optional description; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* status — {draft, open, closed, completed}; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* start\_at — Planned start datetime; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* end\_at — Planned end datetime; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.

* user\_id — Organizer user (FK to User); unique: no; single-value; simple; stored. 

### **ENTRY (strong)**

Attributes:

* entry\_id — Unique identifier; unique: yes; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* name — Entry name (team, movie, etc.); unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* seed — Optional seed integer; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.

* tournament\_id — Owning tournament (FK to Tournament); unique: no; single-value; simple; stored. 

* description — display simple entry description to users; unique: no; single-value; simple; stored.

* image\_url — link to display image (TEXT/URL); unique: no; single-value; simple; stored.

### **MATCHUP (strong)**

Attributes:

* matchup\_id — Unique identifier; unique: yes; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* round\_number — Round index starting at 1; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* opens\_at — Voting window open; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* closes\_at — Voting window close; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* status — {scheduled, open, closed}; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.11

* tournament\_id — Owning tournament (FK to Tournament); unique: no; single-value; simple; stored. 

### **MATCHUP\_ENTRY (associative between MATCHUP and ENTRY)**

Attributes:

* slot — Which side {A, B}; unique within one matchup; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* Identifying keys inherited from MATCHUP and ENTRY.

* Primary Key: (matchup\_id, entry\_id)

* Foreign Keys: matchup\_id → MatchUp(matchup\_id); entry\_id → Entry(entry\_id)

* Constraint: Unique(matchup\_id, slot) (enforces one A and one B per matchup)

### **VOTE (associative between USER and MATCHUP)**

Depends on: USER, MATCHUP 

Attributes:

* cast\_at — When the vote was placed; unique: no; single‑value; simple; stored.  
* Entry\_id — Chosen entry (FK to Entry); unique: no; single-value; simple; stored.

* Primary Key: (user\_id, matchup\_id) one vote per user per matchup.

* Foreign Keys: user\_id → User(user\_id); matchup\_id → MatchUp(matchup\_id); entry\_id → Entry(entry\_id)

* Constraint: (matchup\_id, entry\_id) must exist in MatchUp\_Entry(matchup\_id, entry\_id).

## **1.2.2 – Relationship Descriptions**

Organizes (USER–TOURNAMENT)

* Description: A user creates and manages tournaments.  
* Entities involved: USER, TOURNAMENT  
* Cardinality: 1:M (one user, many tournaments).  
* Participation: TOURNAMENT is mandatory/one; USER is optional/many.

* Attributes: none

For (MATCHUP-VOTE)

* Description: Each vote is tied to one specific matchup; a matchup can have many votes.  
* Entities involved: MATCHUP, VOTE  
* Cardinality: 1:M (one matchup, many votes).  
* Participation: MATCHUP is optional/many; VOTE is mandatory/one.

* Attributes: none

* Constraints: PK(VOTE) \= (user\_id, matchup\_id) enforces one vote per (user, matchup); FK (matchup\_id, entry\_id) → MATCHUP\_ENTRY

ChosenBy (ENTRY-VOTE)

* Description: Each vote chooses exactly one entry; an entry may be chosen by many votes or none.  
* Entities involved: ENTRY, VOTE  
* Cardinality: 1:M (one entry, many votes).  
* Participation: ENTRY is optional/many; VOTE is mandatory/one.

* Attributes: none

* Constraints: FK (matchup\_id, entry\_id) → MATCHUP\_ENTRY (the chosen entry must be one of that matchup’s two entries.

Has (TOURNAMENT–ENTRY)

* Description: A tournament contains entries (contestants) that participate in its bracket.   
* Entities Involved: TOURNAMENT, ENTRY  
* Cardinality: 1:M (TOURNAMENT: ENTRY)  
* Participation: ENTRY is mandatory/one; TOURNAMENT is optional/many.

* Attributes: none

Includes (TOURNAMENT–MATCHUP)

* Description: A tournament is composed of matchups (bracketed contests).  
* Entities Involved: TOURNAMENT, MATCHUP  
* Cardinality: 1:M (TOURNAMENT: MATCHUP)  
* Participation: MATCHUP is mandatory/one; TOURNAMENT is optional/many.

* Attributes: none

Casts (USER–MATCHUP–ENTRY via VOTE)

* Description: A user casts one vote in a specific matchup, selecting one of that matchup’s two entries; stored in the associative entity ‘Vote’.  
* Entities Involved: User, MatchUp (chosen Entry referenced on Vote).  
* Cardinality: M:N (User: MatchUp); uniqueness per (user, matchup).  
* Participation: User is optional/many; MatchUp is optional/many.   
* Relationship attribute: cast\_at on VOTE.  
* Constraints: PK(Vote) \= (user\_id, matchup\_id); FK (matchup\_id, entry\_id) → MatchUp\_Entry (vote must target one of that matchup’s two entries); if tied at close, lower seed advances. 

Includes\_Pairing (MATCHUP–MATCHUP\_ENTRY)

* Description: A matchup has pairing rows in MatchUp\_Entry.  
* Entities Involved: MatchUp, MatchUp\_Entry.  
* Cardinality: 1:M (MatchUp: MatchUp\_Entry).  
* Participation: MatchUp is mandatory/many; MatchUp\_Entry is mandatory/one.  
* Relationship attribute: none

Appears\_In (ENTRY, MATCHUP\_ENTRY)

* Description: An entry appears in pairing rows in MatchUp\_Entry.  
* Entities Involved: Entry, MatchUp\_Entry.  
* Cardinality: 1:M (Entry:MatchUp\_Entry)  
* Participation: Entry is optional/many; MatchUp\_Entry is mandatory/one.  
* Relationship attribute: none.

## **1.2.3 – ER Diagram**

Notation: Crow’s Foot with look‑across labels. Model USER, TOURNAMENT, ENTRY, MATCHUP, MATCHUP\_ENTRY (associative), and VOTE (associative). Draw relationships and cardinalities as described. Ensure that the USER includes a unique user\_id and a password attribute.

**ERD Notes: Each Matchup has exactly two entries (slots A/B). There is one vote per (User, Matchup). VOTE.entry\_id must be one of the two entries paired in that matchup.**

# **Phase 2 – Conversion from Conceptual to Relational Database** {#phase-2-–-conversion-from-conceptual-to-relational-database}

## **2.1 \- Revisions to ER Diagram** {#2.1---revisions-to-er-diagram}

Our group opted to keep our ER Diagram as it was during our submission of Phase 1\. We had no changes we wished to make as of this time, and figured that if anything came up, we would make changes accordingly. For now, the ER Diagram remains the same. 

## **2.2 \- Conceptual to Logical Conversion Process** {#2.2---conceptual-to-logical-conversion-process}

### **2.2.1 \- Converting Entity Types to Relations** {#2.2.1---converting-entity-types-to-relations}

**Strong Entity Types:** 

Tournament (tournament\_id PK, status, description, title, start\_At, end\_At)

User (user\_id PK, role, email, password, display\_name)

MatchUp (matchup\_iD PK, status, round\_number, opens\_at, closes\_At)

Entry ( entry\_id PK, name, seed, description, image\_URL)

**Weak Entity Types:** 

MatchUp\_Entry(matchup\_id PK/FK, entry\_id PK/FK, slot(a,b))

Vote (user\_id PK/FK, matchup\_id PK/FK, entry\_id PK/FK, cast\_At)

Both of these are associative entities, which are a type of weak entity that relies on strong entities for identification. They use composite primary keys made up of foreign keys referencing their parent relations. MatchUp\_Entry references the primary keys of MatchUp and Entry, with ‘slot’ included as an attribute to indicate position within the matchup vote. Vote references the primary keys of User, MatchUp, and Entry, with ‘cast\_at’ included to record when the vote was made. 

**Inheritance:**

Our ER model does not use inheritance (specialization/generalization), so conversion strategies 8a–8d are not needed.

### **2.2.2 \- Converting Relationship Types to Relations** {#2.2.2---converting-relationship-types-to-relations}

**Binary 1:M relationships**

Organizes (User–Tournament):

Implemented by a ‘user\_id’ foreign key in Tournament. Each Tournament must be organized by one Organizer, where their role as a normal user or an organizer will be determined by the role in the User relation. So only the Users with their roles assigned as organizers can be part of the Tournament relation and organize the tournaments.

Has (Tournament–Entry)

This is a 1:M relationship, where one Tournament has many Entries, but each Entry belongs to exactly one Tournament. To represent this, tournament\_id is included as a foreign key in the Entry relation, referencing Tournament(tournament\_id).

Includes (Tournament–Entry):

This is a 1:M relationship, where one Tournament includes many MatchUps, but each MatchUp belongs to exactly one Tournament. To represent this, tournament\_id is added as a foreign key in the MatchUp relation, referencing Tournament(tournament\_id).

**Binary 1:M relationships within Associative Entities**

Includes\_Pairing (MatchUp–MatchUp\_Entry):

Each MatchUp consists of exactly two MatchUp\_Entries, but each MatchUp\_Entry belongs to exactly one MatchUp. To show this, matchup\_id is included in MatchUp\_Entry as a foreign key referencing MatchUp(matchup\_id). The composite key (matchup\_id, entry\_id) ensures the uniqueness of the pairing. 

Appears\_In (Entry–MatchUp\_Entry):

Each Entry appears in many MatchUp\_Entries, but each MatchUp\_Entry corresponds to exactly one Entry. So, MatchUp\_Entry has a foreign key entry\_id referencing Entry(entry\_id).

Vote (User–MatchUp–Entry):

Vote appears to be a ternary relationship among User, MatchUp, and Entry. In the relational model, it is represented as its own relation with foreign keys to each of the three parent relations: Vote(user\_id PK/FK, matchup\_id PK/FK, entry\_id PK/FK, cast\_at).

The point to note here is that the Vote relation references these three, but each Vote is linked to exactly one User, one MatchUp, and one Entry at a time, representing 1:M relationships rather than M: N or a ternary relation. This enforces that each user can vote once per entry per matchup, where cast\_at is a non-key attribute indicating the vote time.

**Multi-valued attributes:**

No multi-valued attributes are present in the models, and each attribute is atomic.

**N-ary relationships:**

Our model does not incorporate n-ary or ternary relationships. While the "Vote" relation might appear to be one, it is instead represented by multiple one-to-many (1:M) relationships: User to Vote, MatchUp to Vote, and Entry to Vote. This structure is a direct result of our ER diagram's design, which reflects our product's business logic. Specifically, this allows each User, MatchUp, and Entry to be associated with multiple votes.

**2.3 \- Results of ER to Relational Conversion**

### **2.3.1 Relation Schema** {#2.3.1-relation-schema}

**![][image2]**

### **Semantic Constraints/Business Rules** {#semantic-constraints/business-rules}

Each matchup must have exactly two contestants, one in slot A and one in slot B. While the database can prevent duplicate slots, it cannot ensure that both slots are filled before publishing a matchup. From a business perspective, this means organizers must check that both slots are occupied before opening the matchup to the public.

Each user may only cast one vote per matchup, and that vote must be submitted while the matchup is open. Votes submitted before the open time or after the closing time are not valid. The application must enforce this rule because the database itself cannot check timestamps against the current time.

The entry that receives a vote must be one of the two contestants in that matchup. If admins later change the pairing of entries, any existing votes may no longer match the correct contestants. In this case, those votes must be intentionally resolved or voided by administrators.

Tournaments must follow a single-elimination format and begin with an even number of entries (preferably a power of two). The database cannot enforce this requirement, so it is the responsibility of organizers to ensure proper tournament setup. In the event of a tie after voting closes, the entry with the lower seed automatically advances, which is a business rule outside the scope of the relational model.

Finally, only users with the role of organizer may create or edit tournaments. General users are limited to browsing tournaments and voting in matchups when they are open.

# **Phase 3 – Physical Implementation and Query Design** {#phase-3-–-physical-implementation-and-query-design}

## **3.0 \- Revisions to the Relational Model** {#3.0---revisions-to-the-relational-model}

Since Phase 2, we revised our relational model to simplify the representation of matchups. At first, we used an associative entity ‘Matchup\_Entry’ to link entries to matchups. Following the instructor's feedback, we decided to eliminate that table and instead added two foreign keys (entryA\_id and entryB\_id) directly in the Matchup table to represent the two competing entries. This change made queries simpler to write. All other tables remained consistent with Phase 2, but we renamed user \-\> users to avoid conflicts with reserved keywords and ensure cleaner references in foreign keys. 

![][image3]

## **3.1 \- Database Implementation** {#3.1---database-implementation}

### **3.1.1 Conversion Process** {#3.1.1-conversion-process}

An issue we ran into was holding our multivalued attributes. That is when we landed on the ENUM data type, which is recommended for storing strings and is accessed by their index, which works for columns like ‘role’ in the table ‘users’. We did not change the primary key of any relation when implementing them as tables. Our group did not encounter many difficulties translating the relational schema to SQL. 

When unsure of implementation, we reference the MariaDB documentation to finalize decisions for issues. 

The kinds of data we inserted into our tables may consist of date, time, emails, IDs, and titles, to name a few. Data collected was generated by ChatGPT and then used to populate our tables. Our tables hold mock data and do not represent anything in the real world, though it is similar in appearance to real data.

### **3.1.2 Schema** {#3.1.2-schema}

Our database schema is implemented through a set of three SQL scripts located in our shared Artemis workspace under the ‘fantasytourneydb’ directory. These scripts allow us to drop, recreate, and repopulate the database at any time for testing or demonstration. Each file serves a distinct purpose as described below.

**Tables.sql:** This file contains all CREATE TABLE statements for the database, including primary keys, foreign keys, and integrity constraints. Before creating new tables, existing ones are dropped to prevent duplication. 

**CODE:**

| `select "Creating the Fantasy Tourney DB tables. "; select "Creating tables with no foreign keys first: User"; drop table if exists vote; drop table if exists matchup; drop table if exists entry; drop table if exists tournament; drop table if exists users; -- create User table create table users (     user_id int primary key auto_increment,     email varchar(255) unique not null check(email <> ''),     role ENUM('admin', 'player', 'guest') not null,     displayname varchar(100) not null check(displayname <> ''),     password varchar(255) not null check(password <> '') ); -- create Tournament table create table tournament (     tournament_id int primary key auto_increment,     title varchar (255) unique not null check(title <> ''),     description varchar(255) not null check(description <> ''),     start_at date not null,     end_at date default null,     tourneystatus ENUM('Upcoming', 'Active', 'Completed') not null,     user_id int not null,     foreign key (user_id) references users(user_id) ); -- create Entry table create table entry (     entry_id int primary key auto_increment,     name varchar(100) not null check(name <> ''),     description varchar(255) default null,     image_URL  varchar(255) default null,     seed int default null,     tournament_id int not null,     foreign key (tournament_id) references tournament(tournament_id) ); -- create MatchUp table create table matchup (     matchup_id int primary key auto_increment,     round_number int not null,     status enum('Upcoming', 'Active', 'Completed') not null,     opens_at datetime not null,     closes_at datetime not null,     tournament_id int not null,     entryA_id int not null,      entryB_id int not null,      foreign key (tournament_id) references tournament(tournament_id),     foreign key (entryA_id) references entry(entry_id),     foreign key (entryB_id) references entry(entry_id),     check (entryA_id <> entryB_id) ); -- create Vote table; create table vote (     user_id int not null,     matchup_id int not null,     entry_id int not null,     cast_at datetime default current_timestamp,      primary key (user_id, matchup_id),     foreign key (user_id) references users(user_id),     foreign key (matchup_id) references matchup(matchup_id),     foreign key (entry_id) references entry(entry_id) );`  |
| :---- |

### **3.2.1 Q1:** {#3.2.1-q1:}

**PE:** Find tournaments with ‘Winter Clash’ as the title.  
**RA:** T ← σ title \= “basketball” (Tournament)

| `SELECT *  FROM tournament  WHERE title = 'Winter Clash';` |

### **3.2.2 Q2:** {#3.2.2-q2:}

**PE:** Find users who are tournament organizers.  
**RA:** U ← σ role \= “organizer” (User)  
RESULT ← π display\_name (U)

| `SELECT displayname FROM users WHERE role = 'admin';` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.3 Q3:** {#3.2.3-q3:}

**PE:** Find the names of entries that start at 11 AM.  
**RA:** T ← σ start\_at \= "11 AM" (Tournament)  
 E ← T ⋈ T.tournament\_id \= Entry.tournament\_id Entry  
 RESULT ← π name (E)  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT e.name FROM tournament t JOIN entry e ON t.tournament_id = e.tournament_id WHERE t.start_at = '11:00:00';` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.4 Q4:** {#3.2.4-q4:}

**PE:** Find the emails of users who cast votes on the matchup with ID 214324\.  
**RA:** V ← σmatchup\_id \= "214324" (Vote)  
 U ← V ⋈ V.user\_id \= User.user\_id User  
 RESULT ← π email (U)  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT u.email FROM vote v JOIN users u ON v.user_id = u.user_id WHERE v.matchup_id = 214324;` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.5 Q5:** {#3.2.5-q5:}

**PE:** Show all votes and who voted for what  
**RA:** πdisplayname, matchup\_id, name, cast\_at​((( Vote ⋈Vote.user\_id=Users.user\_id​ Users ) ⋈Vote.matchup\_id=Matchup.matchup\_id​ Matchup ) ⨝ Vote.entry\_id \= Entry.entry\_id Entry ) )  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT u.displayname, m.matchup_id, e.name AS voted_for, v.cast_at  FROM vote v  JOIN users u ON v.user_id = u.user_id  JOIN matchup m ON v.matchup_id = m.matchup_id  JOIN entry e ON v.entry_id = e.entry_id;` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.6 Q6:** {#3.2.6-q6:}

**PE:** Show each matchup and the two entries competing  
**RA:** πmatchup\_id, E1.name, E2.name​(( Matchup ⋈Matchup.entryA\_id=E1.entry\_id​ ρE1​(Entry) ) ⋈Matchup.entryB\_id=E2.entry\_id​ ρE2​(Entry))  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT m.matchup_id, e1.name AS entry_A, e2.name AS entry_B  FROM matchup m  JOIN entry e1 ON m.entryA_id = e1.entry_id  JOIN entry e2 ON m.entryB_id = e2.entry_id;` |
| :---- |

### 

### **3.2.6 Q7:** {#3.2.6-q7:}

**PE:**  List all tournaments and their creators  
**RA:** πtitle, displayname​( Tournament ⋈Tournament.user\_id=Users.user\_id​ Users )  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT t.title, u.displayname AS created_by  FROM tournament t  JOIN users u ON t.user_id = u.user_id;` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.8 Q8:** {#3.2.8-q8:}

**PE:** Find the tournament that has the highest average number of votes per matchup  
**RA:** T1 ← γ matchup\_id; count(user\_id)→vote\_count (Vote)  
 T2 ← T1 ⋈ T1.matchup\_id \= Matchup.matchup\_id Matchup  
 Tavg ← γ tournament\_id; avg(vote\_count)→avg\_votes (T2)  
 Tmax ← σ avg\_votes \= MAX(avg\_votes) (Tavg)  
 R ← Tmax ⋈ Tmax.tournament\_id \= Tournament.tournament\_id Tournament  
 R ← π title (R)  
**SQL:**

| `WITH votes_per_matchup AS (     SELECT matchup_id, COUNT(user_id) AS vote_count     FROM vote     GROUP BY matchup_id ), avg_votes_per_tournament AS (     SELECT m.tournament_id, AVG(v.vote_count) AS avg_votes     FROM votes_per_matchup v     JOIN matchup m ON v.matchup_id = m.matchup_id     GROUP BY m.tournament_id ) SELECT t.title FROM avg_votes_per_tournament a JOIN tournament t ON a.tournament_id = t.tournament_id WHERE a.avg_votes = (     SELECT MAX(avg_votes) FROM avg_votes_per_tournament );` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.3 Q9:** {#3.2.3-q9:}

**PE:** Find users who have never cast a vote  
**RA:** T1 ← π user\_id (User)  
 T2 ← π user\_id (Vote)  
 R ← T1 \- T2  
**SQL:**

| `SELECT u.user_id, u.email FROM users u WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (     SELECT v.user_id FROM vote v );` |
| :---- |

### **3.2.10 Q10:** {#3.2.10-q10:}

**PE:**  To identify users who have not voted in every open matchup in a tournament   
**RA:**       OpenMatchups ←π matchup\_id (σ status \= “open” (Matchup))  
UserVotes ← π user\_id,matchup\_id(σ status \= “open”(Vote ⋈ Matchup))  
	UsersWhoVotedForAll ← UserVotes ÷ OpenMatchups  
	AllUsers ← π user\_id (User)  
	UsersPendingVotes ← AllUsers \- UsersWhoVotedForAll  
**SQL:**

| `-- Users who have not voted in every open matchup WITH open_matchups AS (     SELECT matchup_id     FROM matchup     WHERE status = 'open' ), user_votes AS (     SELECT v.user_id, v.matchup_id     FROM vote v     JOIN matchup m ON v.matchup_id = m.matchup_id     WHERE m.status = 'open' ), users_voted_all AS (     SELECT uv.user_id     FROM user_votes uv     GROUP BY uv.user_id     HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT uv.matchup_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM open_matchups) ) SELECT u.user_id, u.email FROM users u WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM users_voted_all);`  |
| :---- |

# **Phase 4 – Programming Logic for SQL** {#phase-4-–-programming-logic-for-sql}

## **4.1 \- Introduction** {#4.1---introduction}

SQL programming logic is different from other languages because it relies on an existing structure. This structure is also known as a relational database. Queries cannot be executed without knowledge of the existing tables and how they are connected through primary and foreign keys. SQL statements will work in appropriate environments however the same queries will not run everywhere. 

* View (fetches data from tables and is presented in a customized format)  
1. Giving users an abstracted layer allows them to easily make an account and provide tournaments for the community to participate in  
2. Allows control of  data access points which is crucial for security reasons

   

* Triggers (SQL statements that are invoked when an event occurs on a table.)  
1. Save results of the current match when the voting window is closes

   

* Stored Procedures (Recurring SQL query)  
1. INSERT Tournament  
2. INSERT Account  
3. UPDATE Tournament  
4. UPDATE Account

## **4.2 \- Views** {#4.2---views}

This section presents three SQL views created for our Fantasy Tournament application. Each view includes the SQL command used to create it, a description of why the view is useful, and an example query using the view with its returned results. These views simplify repeated queries and support features that will be used in the future. 

### **4.2.1 View 1: *view\_active\_tournaments*** {#4.2.1-view-1:-view_active_tournaments}

The application frequently needs to display a list of currently active tournaments. Instead of rewriting a long SELECT statement every time, this view merges the logic. It improves readability, reduces repeated SQL code, and supports fast filtering during tournament browsing. 

| `-- View 1 CREATE VIEW view_active_tournaments AS SELECT      tournament_id,     title,     description,     start_at,     end_at,     tourneystatus,     user_id FROM tournament WHERE tourneystatus = 'active';`  |
| :---- |

| `-- Sample Query  SELECT title, start_at, end_at FROM view_active_tournaments ORDER BY start_at ASC; -- Shows active tournaments in order of their start date.  -- Results:  +--------------------------+---------------------------+-----------------+ |        title             |         start_at          |      end_at     | +--------------------------+-----------------+---------------------------| | Best 90s Movie           |       2024-11-01          |       NULL      | | Greatest Video Game      |       2024-11-10          |       NULL      |  +--------------------------+---------------------------------------------+` |
| :---- |

### **4.2.2 View 2: *view\_tournament\_entries*** {#4.2.2-view-2:-view_tournament_entries}

Entries appear throughout the application—in matchups, brackets, leaderboards, and tournament details. Since the system frequently needs to list entries for a specific tournament, this view puts that logic into a single reusable component. It simplifies queries for displaying tournament contents in the GUI and reduces repeated JOIN statements.

| `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS view_tournament_entries; CREATE VIEW view_tournament_entries AS SELECT      t.tournament_id,     t.title AS tournament_title,     e.entry_id,     e.name AS entry_name,     e.image_url FROM tournament t JOIN entry e ON t.tournament_id = e.tournament_id ORDER BY t.tournament_id, e.entry_id;`   |
| :---- |

| `-- Sample Query  SELECT tournament_title, entry_id, entry_name FROM view_tournament_entries WHERE tournament_id = 1; -- Retrieves all entries belonging to tournament #1, including the tournament -- title, each entry’s ID and each entry’s name.  -- Results: +--------------------------+----------+---------------+ | tournament_title         | entry_id | entry_name    | +--------------------------+----------+---------------+ | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        1 | Pepperoni     | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        2 | Mushrooms     | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        3 | Sausage       | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        4 | Green Peppers | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        5 | Onions        | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        6 | Black Olives  | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        7 | Extra Cheese  | | Best Pizza Toppings 2024 |        8 | Bacon         | +--------------------------+----------+---------------+`  |
| :---- |

### **4.2.3 \- View 3: *active\_matchups\_with\_votes*** {#4.2.3---view-3:-active_matchups_with_votes}

Displays all the active matchups with real-time vote counts for each competitor(entry). This view can be used to view live voting result of active tournaments on the frontend , maybe is the admin want to see live progress

| `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS active_matchups_with_votes; CREATE VIEW active_matchups_with_votes AS SELECT      m.matchup_id,     t.tournament_id,     t.title AS tournament_title,     m.round_number,     m.status,     m.opens_at,     m.closes_at,     e1.entry_id AS entryA_id,     e1.name AS entryA_name,     e1.image_URL AS entryA_image,     e2.entry_id AS entryB_id,     e2.name AS entryB_name,     e2.image_URL AS entryB_image,     COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN v.entry_id = m.entryA_id THEN v.user_id END) AS entryA_votes,     COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN v.entry_id = m.entryB_id THEN v.user_id END) AS entryB_votes,     COUNT(DISTINCT v.user_id) AS total_votes FROM matchup m JOIN tournament t ON m.tournament_id = t.tournament_id JOIN entry e1 ON m.entryA_id = e1.entry_id JOIN entry e2 ON m.entryB_id = e2.entry_id LEFT JOIN vote v ON m.matchup_id = v.matchup_id WHERE m.status = 'Active' GROUP BY      m.matchup_id, t.tournament_id, t.title, m.round_number,      m.status, m.opens_at, m.closes_at,     e1.entry_id, e1.name, e1.image_URL,     e2.entry_id, e2.name, e2.image_URL;`   |
| :---- |

| `-- A useful sample query on this view -> SELECT tournament_title, round_number, entryA_name, entryA_votes,entryB_name,         entryB_votes, closes_at FROM active_matchups_with_votes ORDER BY closes_at ASC;` |
| :---- |

## **4.3 \- Stored Procedures** {#4.3---stored-procedures}

#### ***4.3.1. register\_user() \- INSERT*** {#4.3.1.-register_user()---insert}

This procedure handles new user registration with validation. Ensures email uniqueness and proper data formatting before creating an account. Also ensures data integrity by checking for empty fields, validating role values, and preventing the insertion of duplicate email registrations. This handles the entire workflow of a new user creation in a single atomic operation

This procedure will be called from the signup page on the frontend. When the user submits the registration form, the GUI application will execute this procedure with the user-provided credentials. The procedure performs all the server-side validation, thus preventing any invalid data from entering the database and providing necessary error messages for the user interface to display on the website.

| `DELIMITER // CREATE PROCEDURE register_user(     p_email VARCHAR (255),     p_password VARCHAR(255),     p_displayname VARCHAR (100),     p_role VARCHAR (20) ) BEGIN      declare email_exists int default 0;     if p_email = "" or p_email is null then         select "ERROR: Email is required" as message;     elseif  p_password = "" or p_password is null then         select "ERROR: Password is required" as message;     elseif p_displayname = "" or p_displayname is null then         select "ERROR: Displayname is required" as message;     elseif p_role not in ("admin", "player", "guest") then         select "ERROR: Invalid Role" as message;          else          -- check if email already exists             select count(*) into email_exists             from users             where email = p_email;         if email_exists > 0 then             select "ERROR: Email already exists" as message;         else             insert into users (email, password, displayname, role)             values (p_email, p_password, p_displayname, p_role);             -- returning successfully inserted user info row             select "User registered successfully!" as message;             select * from users              where email = p_email;         end if;     end if;  END // DELIMITER ;` |
| :---- |

**Command to execute procedure:** 

| `CALL register_user('newuser@gmail.com', 'securepwd123', 'NewUser', 'Player');` |
| :---- |

#### ***4.3.2. delete\_tournament() \- DELETE*** {#4.3.2.-delete_tournament()---delete}

Safely deletes old tournaments if admins want to and also all of the associated data (entries, matchups, votes) relating to that specific tournament in a single transaction. Validation prevents deletion of active tournaments.

This procedure was created in order to safely remove the tournaments and all associated data (entries, matchups, votes) in the correct order with respect to foreign key relationships. It includes business logic to prevent deletion of active tournaments, protecting ongoing tournaments where players are competing from accidental removal.

This procedure is planned to be used by the application’s administrators to clean up old/completed tournaments if they feel that they are no longer needed. Thus, removing archived tournaments takes up waste space and all related data, maintaining foreign key referential integrities at the same time, preventing deletion of tournaments that are still in progress

| `DELIMITER // CREATE PROCEDURE delete_tournament(     p_tournament_id INT  ) BEGIN      DECLARE tournament_exists int default 0;      DECLARE tournament_status varchar(30);     DECLARE active_matchup_count int default 0;     -- check if tournament exists         select count(*) into tournament_exists         from tournament          where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;     if tournament_exists = 0 then         select "Error: Tournament does not exist/ not found" as message;     else         -- get the status of tournament         select tourneystatus into tournament_status         from tournament          where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;         -- checking if tournament as active matchups         select count(*) into active_matchup_count         from matchup         where tournament_id = p_tournament_id         and status = "Active";         if tournament_status = "Active" then                select "Error: Cannot delete an active tournament" as message;         elseif active_matchup_count > 0 then             select concat("Error: Cannot delete tournament with",                            active_matchup_count, "active matchup(s). Cancel them first") as message;         else             -- everything is okay to delete right now             delete from vote             where matchup_id in (                 select matchup_id from matchup where tournament_id = p_tournament_id             );             delete from matchup where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;             delete from entry where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;             delete from tournament where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;             select concat("Tournament Id ", p_tournament_id, " and related data are deleted") as message;         end if;     end if; END // DELIMITER ;` |
| :---- |

**Command to execute procedure:** 

| `CALL delete_tournament(1);` |
| :---- |

![][image6]  
![][image7]  
![][image8]

#### ***4.3.3 update\_matchup\_status() \- UPDATE*** {#4.3.3-update_matchup_status()---update}

The procedure allows control of the entire phase of the matchups, ie, right from creation to completion of each matchup by updating their status based on the primary key (matchup\_id). Matchup progresses through 3 phases: ‘Upcoming’, ‘Active’, ‘Completed’. This procedure provides controlled state changes of matchup status with validation to prevent invalid status values and redundant updates.

Administrators of the application use this procedure to manage the tournament flow. When a round is ready to begin, the admin sets matchups to ‘Active’ to open voting. After voting closes, the admin can mark matchups as ‘Completed’. This can be integrated with one of the admin dashboards, which serves as a control over how the matchup rounds are paced throughout the tournament. In the upcoming GUI development (phase 5), this could be automated based on the opens\_at and closes\_at timestamps, as well as serve as manual control for the admin, allowing flexibility to alter changes to the tournament as the admin desires.

| `DELIMITER // CREATE PROCEDURE update_matchup_status(     p_matchup_id INT,     p_new_status varchar(30) ) BEGIN     DECLARE matchup_exists INT DEFAULT 0;     DECLARE old_status VARCHAR (30);     DECLARE tournament_title VARCHAR (255);     -- check if matchup exist     select count(*) into matchup_exists     from matchup     where matchup_id = p_matchup_id;     if matchup_exists = 0 then          select "Error: Matchup not found" as message;     elseif p_new_status NOT IN ('Upcoming', 'Active', 'Completed') THEN         -- Validation check for allowed status         SELECT CONCAT('Error: Invalid status "', p_new_status,                       '". Allowed values: Upcoming, Active, Completed.') AS message;     else         -- get current status and tournament info          select m.status         into old_status         from matchup m          where m.matchup_id = p_matchup_id;         -- check if new status is passed in the param         if old_status = p_new_status then             select concat("Issue: Matchup id: ", p_matchup_id, " is already in status '", p_new_status, "' ") as message;         else              -- update the status             update matchup              set status = p_new_status             where matchup_id = p_matchup_id;             SELECT CONCAT('Matchup ', p_matchup_id, ' updated successfully!') AS message;         end if;     end if;      END // DELIMITER ;`  |
| :---- |

**Command to execute procedure:** 

| `CALL update_matchup_status(49, 'Active');` |
| :---- |

**![][image9]**

**![][image10]**

#### ***4.3.4 get\_tournament\_stats() \- procedure for statistical metrics*** {#4.3.4-get_tournament_stats()---procedure-for-statistical-metrics}

This procedure generates comprehensive statistical reports for a specific tournament, providing insights into participation rates, voting patterns, and entry popularity. This combines multiple complex queries into a single procedure call, making it easier to retrieve analytics on an entire tournament.

This procedure can serve multiple purposes; administrators can use it to monitor tournament engagement and identify popular entries, users can view tournament statistics on a result/summary page, and view their results or maybe compare their opinions/options with the overall outcome of how the tournament turned out.

| `DELIMITER // CREATE PROCEDURE get_tournament_stats(     p_tournament_id int  ) BEGIN     DECLARE tournament_exists INT DEFAULT 0;          -- Check if tournament exists     select count(*) into tournament_exists     from tournament     where tournament_id = p_tournament_id;          if tournament_exists = 0 then         select 'Error: Tournament not found' as message;              else         -- Tournament Overview         select              t.tournament_id,             t.title,             t.description,             t.tourneystatus,             t.start_at,             t.end_at,             DATEDIFF(COALESCE(t.end_at, now()), t.start_at) as duration_days,             u.displayname as created_by_admin         from tournament t         join users u ON t.user_id = u.user_id         where t.tournament_id = p_tournament_id;                  -- Participation Statistics         select              count(DISTINCT e.entry_id) as total_entries,             count(DISTINCT m.matchup_id) as total_matchups,             count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN m.status = 'Completed' THEN m.matchup_id END) as completed_matchups,             count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN m.status = 'Active' THEN m.matchup_id END) as active_matchups,             count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN m.status = 'Upcoming' THEN m.matchup_id END) as upcoming_matchups,             count(DISTINCT v.user_id) as unique_voters,             count(v.user_id) as total_votes,             round(count(v.user_id) / nullif(count(DISTINCT m.matchup_id), 0), 2) as avg_votes_per_matchup,             max(m.round_number) as max_round_reached         from tournament t         left join entry e on t.tournament_id = e.tournament_id         left join matchup m on t.tournament_id = m.tournament_id         left join vote v on m.matchup_id = v.matchup_id         where t.tournament_id = p_tournament_id;                  -- Top 5 Most Popular Entries         select              e.entry_id,             e.name AS entry_name,             e.seed,             count(v.user_id) AS total_votes_received,             count(DISTINCT m.matchup_id) AS matchups_participated         from entry e         left join vote v on e.entry_id = v.entry_id         left join matchup m on (e.entry_id = m.entryA_id OR e.entry_id = m.entryB_id)         where e.tournament_id = p_tournament_id         group by e.entry_id, e.name, e.seed         order by total_votes_received desc         limit 5;                  -- Vote Distribution by Round         select              m.round_number,             count(DISTINCT m.matchup_id) as matchups_in_round,             count(v.user_id) as votes_in_round,             round(count(v.user_id) / nullif(count(DISTINCT m.matchup_id), 0), 2) as avg_votes_per_matchup         from matchup m         left join vote v on m.matchup_id = v.matchup_id         where m.tournament_id = p_tournament_id         group by m.round_number         order by m.round_number;     end if;      END // DELIMITER ;` |
| :---- |

**Command to execute procedure:** 

| `CALL get_tournament_stats(2);` |
| :---- |

**![][image11]**

## **4.4 \- Triggers** {#4.4---triggers}

In this section, we reviewed all foreign keys used in our schema and ensured that each constraint included appropriate ON UPDATE and ON DELETE behaviors. These rules help maintain referential integrity and simplify cascading deletions throughout the application. 

### **4.4.1 \- Foreign Key Constraints**  {#4.4.1---foreign-key-constraints}

Foreign key constraints enforce the relationships between tables in the Fantasy Tournament database and ensure that the system maintains referential integrity throughout all tournament-related operations. These constraints prevent invalid references, enforce parent/child rules between tables, and maintain consistency when data changes.

As part of Phase 4, we reviewed all existing CREATE TABLE statements from Phase 3 and confirmed that all foreign key relationships have already been implemented correctly. These constraints ensure predictable behavior when tournaments, entries, matchups, and votes are inserted, updated, or deleted. 

Below are the foreign key constraints currently enforced in our schema:

1. **Users → Tournament (RESTRICT)**

   Each tournament must belong to a valid user. Because this FK uses the default ON DELETE/ ON UPDATE RESTRICT, a user cannot be deleted while they still have tournaments associated with them. This prevents “ownerless” tournaments and reflects realistic behavior. 

   **SQL Used:** 

| `foreign key (user_id) references users(user_id)` |
| :---- |

2. **Tournament → Entry (RESTRICT)**

   Every entry must belong to an existing tournament. The RESTRICT behavior prevents deleting a tournament while its entries still exist. This protects the integrity of tournament content and prevents accidental loss of entire sets of entries. 

**SQL Used:** 

| `foreign key (tournament_id) references tournament(tournament_id)` |
| :---- |

3. **Tournament/Entry → Matchup (RESTRICT)**

   Matchups depend on both a tournament and two valid entries. The default RESTRICT prevents deleting a tournament if matchups exist and deleting an entry if it is used in any matchup. This prevents matchups from becoming invalid.

   **SQL Used:** 

| `foreign key (tournament_id) references tournament(tournament_id), foreign key(entryA_id) references entry(entry_id), foreign key(entryB_id) references entry(entry_id)` |
| :---- |

4. **Users/Matchup/Entry → Vote (RESTRICT)**

   Votes depend on a valid user, a valid matchup, and a valid entry. All foreign keys use RESTRICT, meaning a matchup cannot be deleted, an entry cannot be deleted if someone voted for it, and a user cannot be deleted if they have cast votes. This preserves the complete voting history. Deleting user accounts will need to be revised and adjusted in Phase 5 to allow the deleted account’s data to persist after the account has been deleted. 

   **SQL Used:** 

| `foreign key (user_id) references users(user_id), foreign key (matchup_id) references matchup(matchup_id), foreign key (entry_id) references entry(entry_id)` |
| :---- |

### **4.4.2 \- Explicit Triggers** {#4.4.2---explicit-triggers}

#### **4.4.2.1 trg\_entry\_same\_ins & trg\_entry\_same\_upd** {#4.4.2.1-trg_entry_same_ins-&-trg_entry_same_upd}

These two triggers work together to strictly enforce unique entry names within a single tournament. trg\_entry\_same\_ins (INSERT) ensures that when a new entry is added, its name does not conflict with an existing entry in the same tournament. trg\_entry\_same\_upd (UPDATE) ensures that when an existing entry is renamed, it is not changed to a name that is already in use by another competitor in that tournament. Together, these triggers protect the integrity of the tournament bracket. If duplicate names were allowed, the GUI visualization would become confusing (e.g., users wouldn't know which "Team A" they were voting for), potentially corrupting the voting results.

| DELIMITER // DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg\_entry\_same\_ins // CREATE TRIGGER trg\_entry\_same\_ins BEFORE INSERT ON entry FOR EACH ROW BEGIN   IF EXISTS (     SELECT 1     FROM entry e     WHERE e.tournament\_id \= NEW.tournament\_id       AND e.name \= NEW.name   ) THEN     SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'       SET MESSAGE\_TEXT \= 'Duplicate entry name in this tournament.';   END IF; END // DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg\_entry\_same\_upd // CREATE TRIGGER trg\_entry\_same\_upd BEFORE UPDATE ON entry FOR EACH ROW BEGIN   IF EXISTS (     SELECT 1     FROM entry e     WHERE e.tournament\_id \= NEW.tournament\_id       AND e.name \= NEW.name       AND e.entry\_id \<\> NEW.entry\_id   ) THEN     SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'       SET MESSAGE\_TEXT \= 'Duplicate entry name in this tournament.';   END IF; END // |
| :---- |

**trg\_entry\_same\_ins:**   
![][image12]  
**trg\_entry\_same\_upd:**   
![][image13]

#### **4.4.2.2 trg\_matchup\_min\_votes\_upd** {#4.4.2.2-trg_matchup_min_votes_upd}

This trigger implements a "Quality Control" rule for our tournaments. Its purpose is to ensure that a matchup cannot be finalized unless it has received at least a minimal level of activity from users (set here to 1 vote). If an administrator or the system attempts to mark a matchup as 'Completed' while the vote count is zero, the trigger raises an exception. This is intended to prevent tournaments from advancing automatically with "empty" results, encouraging administrators to wait for user activity before closing a round. (Tournament no longer needs a minimum number of votes as the lowest seed always advances)

| DELIMITER // DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg\_matchup\_min\_votes\_upd // CREATE TRIGGER trg\_matchup\_min\_votes\_upd BEFORE UPDATE ON matchup FOR EACH ROW BEGIN  IF NEW.status \= 'Completed' AND OLD.status \<\> 'Completed' THEN     IF (SELECT COUNT(\*) FROM vote WHERE matchup\_id \= NEW.matchup\_id) \< 1 THEN       SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'         SET MESSAGE\_TEXT \= 'Cannot complete matchup: minimum vote threshold not met.';     END IF;   END IF; END // DELIMITER ; |
| :---- |

**![][image14]**

#### **4.4.2.3 trg\_matchup\_select\_winner** {#4.4.2.3-trg_matchup_select_winner}

This trigger is designed to automate the business logic of determining a match winner. Instead of writing complex application code to query vote counts, compare them, handle tie-breakers, and then issue a separate update, this trigger handles it all atomically within the database. We intend to use this in the Phase 5 "Round Advancement" logic. When a matchup's time limit expires, the application will simply update the status to 'Completed', and this trigger will instantly calculate the winner based on votes (or seed tie-breakers) and update the winner\_entry\_id. This guarantees that a completed match never exists without a declared result. 

| DELIMITER // DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg\_matchup\_select\_winner // CREATE TRIGGER trg\_matchup\_select\_winner BEFORE UPDATE ON matchup FOR EACH ROW BEGIN   DECLARE votesA INT DEFAULT 0;   DECLARE votesB INT DEFAULT 0;   DECLARE seedA  INT DEFAULT NULL;   DECLARE seedB  INT DEFAULT NULL;   IF NEW.status \= 'Completed' AND OLD.status \<\> 'Completed' THEN     SELECT COUNT(\*)       INTO votesA       FROM vote      WHERE matchup\_id \= NEW.matchup\_id        AND entry\_id   \= NEW.entryA\_id;     SELECT COUNT(\*)       INTO votesB       FROM vote      WHERE matchup\_id \= NEW.matchup\_id        AND entry\_id   \= NEW.entryB\_id;     IF votesA \> votesB THEN       SET NEW.winner\_entry\_id \= NEW.entryA\_id;     ELSEIF votesB \> votesA THEN       SET NEW.winner\_entry\_id \= NEW.entryB\_id;     ELSE       SELECT seed         INTO seedA         FROM entry        WHERE entry\_id \= NEW.entryA\_id;       SELECT seed         INTO seedB         FROM entry        WHERE entry\_id \= NEW.entryB\_id;       SET seedA \= COALESCE(seedA, 9999);       SET seedB \= COALESCE(seedB, 9999);       IF seedA \< seedB THEN         SET NEW.winner\_entry\_id \= NEW.entryA\_id;       ELSEIF seedB \< seedA THEN         SET NEW.winner\_entry\_id \= NEW.entryB\_id;       ELSE         SET NEW.winner\_entry\_id \= NEW.entryA\_id;       END IF;     END IF;   END IF; END // DELIMITER ;  |
| :---- |

**![][image15]**

#### **4.4.2.3 Trg\_entry\_prevent\_delete\_active** {#4.4.2.3-trg_entry_prevent_delete_active}

This trigger acts as a critical safety lock for our data integrity. Once a tournament is marked as 'Active', the bracket structure relies on specific entries being present to link matchups together. Deleting an entry during a live tournament would corrupt the data and likely break the visualization in our future GUI. This trigger is intended to prevent administrators or accidental code execution from removing a competitor while the tournament is ongoing. It forces the tournament to be set to 'Completed' or 'Upcoming' before any structural changes can be made.

| `DELIMITER // CREATE TRIGGER trg_entry_prevent_delete_active BEFORE DELETE ON entry FOR EACH ROW BEGIN     DECLARE tourney_status VARCHAR(20);          -- Check the status of the tournament this entry belongs to     SELECT tourneystatus INTO tourney_status     FROM tournament     WHERE tournament_id = OLD.tournament_id;          -- If tournament is active, block the delete     IF tourney_status = 'Active' THEN         SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'          SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Safety Lock: Cannot delete an entry while the tournament is Active.';     END IF; END // DELIMITER ;` |
| :---- |

![][image16]

# 

# **Phase 5 – Database Programming and Graphical User Interface (GUI) Application Development** {#phase-5-–-database-programming-and-graphical-user-interface-(gui)-application-development}

## **5.0 \- GUI Development** {#5.0---gui-development}

The Fantasy Tourney application supports three user groups: ***Guests, Players,*** and ***Admins.***

* ***Guests*** have read-only access to browse active/upcoming tournaments and view tournament brackets. They cannot vote or create tournaments.   
* ***Players*** are the main users who can create tournaments, vote in active matchups, and manage their personal profiles.   
* ***Admins*** possess overall supervision,  can moderate tournaments, delete tournaments/entries, and delete users. 

### **5.0.1 Examples of CRUD Operations Supported in the GUI** {#5.0.1-examples-of-crud-operations-supported-in-the-gui}

Each user group performs different create, read, update, and delete operations:

**Create:**  
Registering a new account to become a member (guest), and then he becomes a registered player who can create tournaments with 16 entries (player, admin), and can cast votes on matchups when tournaments are active (player, admin).  
**Read:**  
Browsing tournaments and their respective brackets(Guest, Player, Admin). Viewing the full tournament statistics page (Player, Admin). Tournaments created, entries voted on, and participation can be viewed on the profile page (Player). All players and tournaments on the site can be viewed on the Admin panel(Admin).  
**Update:**  
Update profiles, inclusive of unique username, bio, profile picture, and password under the profile page (Player). Update tournament settings like start & end datetimes (Player). Update Tournament statuses, making tournaments end early(Admin).  
**Delete:**   
Delete the tournaments they created(Player). Delete any tournament or user(Admin).

**Report Generation**  
The application generates a detailed statistical report for any tournament, including tournament details, vote distribution by each round in tournaments, participation metrics, and "Top 5 Entries". This report is generated using aggregate functions via the get\_tournament\_stats stored procedure and can be saved as a PDF using the button provided in the tournament stats page, where we use the browser’s native print to PDF option to locally save the tournament statistics as it is on the webpage.

### **5.0.2 Use of Database Programming in the GUI** {#5.0.2-use-of-database-programming-in-the-gui}

The GUI extensively utilizes these forms of database logic handling validated, consistent data and prevents unintended or invalid operations. 

1. **Views** are implemented to simplify complex read operations; for instance, the *view\_active\_tournaments* and *view\_tournament\_summary* views allow the browsing and admin pages to load tournament lists without executing repetitive, complex JOIN queries in the application layer.  
2. **Stored Procedures** manage all atomic transactions: user registration is handled by *register\_user*, tournament creation by *create\_tournament*, and safe deletion by *delete\_tournament*. Finally, the detailed statistical reports on the "Statistics" page are generated entirely by the *get\_tournament\_stats* procedure, which aggregates vote and matchup data on the server side.  
3. **Triggers** help maintain data integrity, on which the GUI indirectly relies. Preventing the insertion of duplicate entry names within the same tournament is done with *Trg\_entry\_same\_ins* and *Trg\_entry\_same\_upd*, ensuring tournament creators cannot create two entries with the same name, preventing bracket inconsistencies. 

### **5.0.3 Database Tables Used** {#5.0.3-database-tables-used}

**Directly Used:**   
The GUI directly uses **users** table for authentication and profile management. The **tournament** and **entry** tables are accessed directly to render the bracket visualization in the player interface and to list out all the tournaments with respect to their statuses. The **matchup** and **vote** tables are heavily utilized during the voting process to record user choices, to progress through each round, show individual player votes, and to display real-time results.

**Indirectly Used:**  
Through views and stored procedures that aggregate or filter tournament information, we do complex aggregations of the **vote** and **matchup** tables are abstracted via views such as *active\_matchups\_with\_votes*, *view\_tournament\_entries*, and *view\_tournament\_summary*. These views allow the Admin Panel and Tournament List to load summaries and status information without executing complex JOINs in the application code. Similarly, the *get\_tournament\_stats* stored procedure encapsulates heavy aggregation logic for the Statistics page, which allows the application layer to retrieve a full statistical report using a single, simple stored procedure call rather than making multiple queries exposing raw table logic to the front end.

## **5.1 \- GUI Functionalities and User Groups** {#5.1---gui-functionalities-and-user-groups}

The Fantasy Tournament GUI supports three user groups: **Guests, Players,** and **Admins**. Each user group interacts with the application differently based on the permissions defined in the database and enforced through the GUI.

***Guests*** have read-only access to public tournament information. They can browse active and upcoming tournaments and view their brackets, but cannot vote or create tournaments. 

***Players*** have full participation access. They can create tournaments, vote in matchups, customize their profiles, and view tournament statistics. Players can also track tournaments they created or voted in.

***Admins*** inherit all Player capabilities but also have access to moderation tools. Admins can delete tournaments or users, end tournaments early, and view administrative data such as all tournaments and all users. 

The Fantasy Tournament GUI adapts dynamically based on the logged-in user's role, ensuring that each group sees only the controls appropriate for their access level.

### **5.1.1 \- User Capabilities**  {#5.1.1---user-capabilities}

**Guest Capabilities-** Unregistered visitors are restricted to a "Read-Only" mode. They can browse the tournament feed to view lists of active, upcoming, and completed tournaments and inspect the brackets of a specific tournament to see live results. However, functionality that requires writing to the database—such as voting or creating tournaments—is disabled, and attempting to access these features redirects them to a "Access Denied" page prompting registration.

**Player Capabilities-** This is the primary user group and has full participation access. Upon logging in, players gain the ability to interact with the database by voting in active matchups during active rounds. They can access a private Profile Dashboard where they can view their voting history, edit their account details (Display Name, Bio, profile picture), and manage tournaments they have created. The "Create Tournament" interface is exclusive to logged-in users, allowing them to upload images, set start and end dates, and define entries for a new bracket.

**Admin Capabilities-** Admins inherit all Player capabilities but have exclusive access to the Admin Panel. This interface allows them to search for any user or tournament. Admins serve a moderation role; they can permanently delete any user or tournament that violates platform rules. These deletion actions cascade through the database to maintain referential integrity.
